metadata.title: Läsförmågan hos svenska elever i årskurs 4 i ett internationellt perspektiv (PIRLS 2016)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: PIRLS 2016 uses a two-stage probability sampling design in which schools are sampled first and then one or two instructional groups/classes are sampled within each selected school; all sampled students are expected to take the assessment. The report states that the student sample is representative with respect to students, and it reports a student response rate of about 95%, implying that analyses should account for the complex survey design when estimating population-level means and differences. The report does not specify the exact weight variable names (e.g., student design weights) or replicate-weight procedures, so the precise implementation details are not documented here. For interpretation of the reported confidence intervals and statistical significance, analysts should use the PIRLS-provided sampling weights and the corresponding variance estimation approach from the PIRLS technical documentation when reproducing results.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This is a national descriptive results report that summarizes PIRLS reading literacy outcomes and questionnaire indices rather than training or evaluating a predictive model with an explicitly stated missing-data strategy. While PIRLS achievement is scaled using PIRLS procedures (including the use of plausible values in the underlying international scoring), this report does not document a specific missing-data handling method for any analytic model. Therefore, missing-data handling is not reported in the text provided, and the appropriate approach is to rely on the official PIRLS scoring and technical documentation for the underlying treatment of missingness.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report focuses on Sweden’s PIRLS 2016 results for students in grade 4 (fourth year in primary school). The PIRLS sampling procedure is described as a two-stage random sample: schools are selected first, then one or two instructional groups/classes within each school. All sampled students are expected to complete the reading assessment, with exceptions for students who cannot participate due to cognitive or physical disabilities or insufficient time in the country to learn enough Swedish to complete the test. The report also notes a student response rate of about 95%. For subsequent subgroup analyses (e.g., gender, socioeconomic background, migration background, reading attitudes), the report excludes very small groups where reliable estimates are not possible (e.g., the 'few resources' socioeconomic group and the 'never/near never' early reading activities group are not included in further analyses).

data.outcome_summary: PIRLS 2016 assesses reading literacy in grade 4 using both literary fiction and informational texts (sachprosa), with items mapped to four comprehension processes (explicitly stated information, simple inferences, interpretive integration, and critical evaluation). In Sweden, PIRLS 2016 was administered with paper-and-pencil tests; each student reads two texts and answers about 25–30 items, enabling reliable national-level estimates while not producing scores for each student on every item. The report uses PIRLS scaling to a common score scale (international mean 500, SD 100 in 2001) and reports uncertainty via confidence intervals and 5% significance testing. Sweden’s mean reading literacy score is 555, which is 16 points above the EU/OECD average (539), and the report describes a statistically significant improvement of 13 points since 2011. It also reports subgroup patterns: girls outperform boys; students with higher home resources for learning outperform those with fewer resources; and migration-related gaps largely attenuate after accounting for socioeconomic background. The report emphasizes that PIRLS is designed for national comparisons and that results should not be interpreted at the individual student or single-school level.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This document is a national descriptive results report for PIRLS 2016 rather than an empirical machine-learning study. It does not train or compare predictive models, and it does not provide an ML target variable, algorithmic pipeline, or model performance metrics. Consequently, fields related to ML techniques and structured predictive findings are intentionally empty, while the report’s value lies in assessment design description and descriptive/statistical comparisons across countries, time points, and questionnaire-based indices.
